My father, Torstein Bakke, wants to go back to the ferry workshop part-time, two days a week, from 24 November. His supervisor, Kjetil Fosse, says light tasks at the bench are possible but nothing that involves crawling under engines, and he asked for a note that can go to the safety officer.

The hip replacement was on 3 October. The surgeon's letter says the joint is stable but the wound healed slowly, with a course of antibiotics that ended last Sunday. He also has type 2 diabetes, which is why the physio wants his blood sugar checked before any session that includes cycling.

Ingeborg Tveit, his physiotherapist, has him on the stationary bike for ten minutes on Tuesdays and Thursdays, plus the stair routine at home every morning. Weight-bearing is full, but he must not twist on the operated leg and he must not sit in low chairs for the first twelve weeks. The next check is on 14 November at the rehab unit in Drammen.

I lost my hours at the bakery in September, and since then my income is a part-time 14,500 kronor a month before tax. I cannot pay the 340 in one go, but I could manage 100 now and the rest in December if the parents' fund will not cover it. Sigrid Palmgren at the office said last year's grant went to families under 15,000 a month.
